name: Sunset
seoDesc: Sunset: work out hemisphere (N/S) from the day and the latitude. A free physics calculator with the formula, units and a worked example.
summary: The Sunset calculator turns the day, the latitude and more into hemisphere (N/S). It is built for a lab report, a problem set or a sanity check on a physical situation. Nothing repaints underneath you: edit a field, press Calculate, and the new answer appears. That is how you find out which input the result is sensitive to.

sections.title: How does the Sunset calculator work?
sections.html:
The Sunset calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports hemisphere (N/S) in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case (the hemisphere (E/W), the time zone and the type of dusk); then you give the day; then you type in the latitude (φ), the longitude (λ) and the latitude (φ) (Hidden).

Press Calculate and the page works through the equation with the values you supplied and derives the rest; it then keeps up with you as you correct a typo.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: What do you need to enter?
sections.html:
• A calendar date. Use the picker; the answer is recalculated the moment the date changes, and the count is done date-to-date rather than by subtracting timestamps.
  • A measured quantity, entered by default in degrees / minutes / seconds. The unit chip switches it to any of the 4 supported units.
  • Pick the option that matches your case — 2 options, such as east and west. The choice changes which relationship the calculator applies, not just a multiplier, so it is worth reading the options carefully.
  • A measured quantity, entered by default in degrees / minutes / seconds. The unit chip switches it to any of the 4 supported units.
  • Pick the option that matches your case — 35 options, such as UTC-12 (International Date Line West), UTC-11 (SST) and UTC-10 (HST). The choice changes which relationship the calculator applies, not just a multiplier, so it is worth reading the options carefully.
  • A single on/off switch — tick it for “Apply daylight savings”, leave it clear for the other case. It changes which relationship the calculator applies, not just a multiplier.
  • Pick the option that matches your case — 4 options, such as sunset, civil and nautical. The choice changes which relationship the calculator applies, not just a multiplier, so it is worth reading the options carefully.
  • A measured quantity, entered by default in degrees. The unit chip switches it to any of the 12 supported units.
  • A plain number with no unit attached.

5 fields on this form are a choice rather than a number. Those choices decide which version of the calculation applies, so they are worth setting before you worry about the digits.

sections.title: The formula behind the Sunset calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Hemisphere (N/S)=latitude (φ) ÷ latitude (φ)
Longitude (λ)=longitude (λ) × hemisphere (E ÷ W)
Dayum=((day))
Sunset time=((day, latitude (φ), longitude (λ), time zone, daylisa, type of dusk, 1))
Is sunset nan=(day, latitude (φ), longitude (λ), time zone, daylisa, type of dusk, 1)
Is sunset ref nan=(day, latitude (φ), longitude (λ), time zone, daylisa, type of dusk, 1)

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

Before doubting the arithmetic, check the inputs: a unit chip on the wrong setting, a drop-down left at its default, or a percentage typed as a whole number rather than a decimal will each shift the answer by a clean power of ten.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Units are handled by conversion rather than by convention. Whatever chip you choose, the number is turned into a single base unit before the calculation and rendered back afterwards, so a form filled with a mixture of systems still gives the right answer.

  • Coordinates, opening in degrees / minutes / seconds
  • Coordinates, opening in degrees / minutes / seconds
  • Time, opening in hours / minutes
  • Time, opening in hours / minutes
  • Angle, opening in degrees
  • Angle, opening in degrees

Display rounding is separate from calculation rounding: the digits you see are shortened, the value behind them is not. Numbers far from everyday size are shown in scientific notation so the significant digits stay readable.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Sunset calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Testing whether an answer is physically plausible before you trust it
  • Writing up a lab result and needing a quick cross-check
  • Solving a problem set where the algebra is more interesting than the arithmetic
  • Any time the same 4 figures keep coming back — the day, the latitude and the longitude — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Write the answer down with its unit. A bare number copied into a report later is exactly where units get lost.
  • Leave the field you want solved for empty rather than guessing at it. Filling every box tells the calculator you already know the answer.
  • Keep the units you enter consistent. Mixing centimetres into a field that expects metres is the single most common way to get an answer that is out by a factor of a hundred.
  • Compare two scenarios by changing the input that actually differs between them, and keep the rest fixed, so the difference you see is the difference you meant to test.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.
  • Dates are compared date to date in your own time zone, so a daylight-saving change will not shift the count by a day.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the Sunset calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns hemisphere (N/S), derived from the day, the latitude and the longitude. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Sunset calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the day, the latitude, the longitude and the latitude (φ), which is 9 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter latitude (φ) in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Latitude (φ) opens in degrees / minutes / seconds and the chip beside it offers 4 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There are several choices to make (5 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

faq.q: Is the Sunset calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
